question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent line to the curve $f(x)=-7\operatorname{arccsc} x$ at $x=\sqrt{5}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the derivative of $\operatorname{arccsc} $ is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccsc} x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Using the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-7\operatorname{arccsc} x) \\  & =-7\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\right) \\  & =\frac{7}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{5}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\sqrt{5}) & =\frac{7}{|\sqrt{5}|\sqrt{{\sqrt{5}}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{7}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5-1}} \\  & =\frac{7}{2\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the derivative of $\operatorname{arccsc} $ is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccsc} x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Using the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}+5\operatorname{arccsc} x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}+5\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccsc} x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}+5\left(-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}-\frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the derivative of $\operatorname{arccot} $ is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccot} x)=-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}.
$$

Using the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccot} x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the derivative of $\operatorname{arccot} $ is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccot} \,x)=-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}.
$$

Using the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+\operatorname{arccot} x) \\  & =2+\left(-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =2-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}(0) & =2-\frac{1}{1+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the derivative of $\operatorname{arccsc} $ is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccsc} x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Using the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}-2\operatorname{arccsc} x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}-2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccsc} x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}-2\left(-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{2}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
The inverse secant derivative is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsec}x)=\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}.
$$

Apply the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y'(x)&=2-3\left(\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}\right)\\
&=2-\frac{3}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the specified input, $|-\sqrt{3}|=\sqrt{3}$ and $(-\sqrt{3})^2-1=2$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
m=y'(-\sqrt{3})&=2-\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{2}}\\
&=2-\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}}\\
&=2-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The absolute value keeps the denominator positive even though the input is negative. Since $-\sqrt{3}<-1$, the derivative exists here.

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
The inverse cosecant derivative is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\operatorname{arccsc}x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}.
$$

Apply the sum, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=2\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\right)-3\left(-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}\right)\\
&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}+\frac{3}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The negative coefficient and the negative inverse cosecant derivative give a positive second term. This derivative is valid for $x>1$, the interior of the function's real domain.

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
The inverse cotangent derivative is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\operatorname{arccot}x)=-\frac{1}{1+x^2}.
$$

Differentiate using the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y'(x)&=2-3\left(-\frac{1}{1+x^2}\right)\\
&=2+\frac{3}{1+x^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent slope is the derivative at the specified input:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m=y'(1)&=2+\frac{3}{1+1^2}\\
&=2+\frac{3}{2}\\
&=\frac{7}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall the derivative of the inverse function:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\operatorname{arccot}x)=-\frac{1}{1+x^2}.
$$

Apply the sum and constant multiple rules, and differentiate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=\frac{1}{1+x^2}+\frac{4x}{1+x^2}\\
&=\frac{4 x + 1}{1+x^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

This derivative is valid for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\operatorname{arccsc}x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}.

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the derivative of $\operatorname{arccot} $ is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(\operatorname{arccot}  x) 	=  -\dfrac 1 {1+x^2}.
$$

Using the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\,\operatorname{arccot} x) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arccot} x) \\  & =2\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =-\frac{2}{1+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we let $u(x)=\operatorname{arccot} x$ and $v(x)={x}^{3},$ and apply the quotient rule.

We use the formulae

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{and}\,{v}^{′}(x)=3{x}^{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\cdot {x}^{3}-\operatorname{arccot} x\cdot 3{x}^{2}}{({x}^{3})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{{x}^{3}}{1+{x}^{2}}-3{x}^{2}\operatorname{arccot} x}{{x}^{6}} \\  & =-\frac{\left(\frac{{x}^{3}+3(1+{x}^{2}){x}^{2}\operatorname{arccot} x}{1+{x}^{2}}\right)}{{x}^{6}} \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{3}+3(1+{x}^{2}){x}^{2}\operatorname{arccot} x}{{x}^{6}(1+{x}^{2})} \\  & =-\frac{x+3(1+{x}^{2})\operatorname{arccot} x}{{x}^{4}(1+{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we let $u(x)={x}^{2}+4x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{arccsc} x,$ and apply the quotient rule.

We use the formulae

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2x+4\,\text{and}\,{v}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2x+4)\cdot \operatorname{arccsc} x-({x}^{2}+4x)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\right)}{{\operatorname{arccsc} }^{2}x} \\  & =\frac{2x+4}{\operatorname{arccsc} x}+\frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot {\operatorname{arccsc} }^{2}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we let $u(x)={3}^{x}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{arccsc} \,x,$ and apply the quotient rule.

We use the formulae

$$
{u}^{′}(x)={3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\,\text{and}\,{v}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3)\cdot \operatorname{arccsc} \,x-{3}^{x}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\right)}{{(\operatorname{arccsc} \,x)}^{2}}. \\  & ={3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot \frac{\operatorname{arccsc} \,x}{{(\operatorname{arccsc} \,x)}^{2}}+\frac{{3}^{x}}{{(\operatorname{arccsc} \,x)}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}} \\  & ={3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{arccsc} \,x}+\frac{{3}^{x}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\frac{1}{|x|{(\operatorname{arccsc} \,x)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we let $u(x)=\operatorname{arccot} x$ and $v(x)=x$, and apply the quotient rule.

We use the formulae

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{and}\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\cdot x-\operatorname{arccot} x\cdot 1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}}-\operatorname{arccot} x}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\left(\frac{x+(1+{x}^{2})\operatorname{arccot} x}{1+{x}^{2}}\right)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{x+(1+{x}^{2})\operatorname{arccot} x}{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the formulae

Therefore,

$$

$$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{arccot}x.$ Their derivatives are

$$
u'(x)=1,\qquad v'(x)=-\frac{1}{1+x^2}.
$$

Applying the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}\\
&=\frac{\operatorname{arccot}x-x\left(-\frac{1}{1+x^2}\right)}{(\operatorname{arccot}x)^2}\\
&=\frac{\operatorname{arccot}x+\frac{x}{1+x^2}}{(\operatorname{arccot}x)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The plus sign before $\frac{x}{1+x^2}$ comes from subtracting $x$ times the negative derivative of $\operatorname{arccot}x.$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u(x)=x^2+2$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{arcsec}x.$ Then

$$
u'(x)=2x,\qquad v'(x)=\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}.
$$

Using the quotient rule,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}\\
&=\frac{2x\operatorname{arcsec}x-(x^2+2)\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}}{(\operatorname{arcsec}x)^2}\\
&=2x\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{arcsec}x}-\frac{x^2+2}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\,\frac{1}{|x|(\operatorname{arcsec}x)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first blank is $2x$ and the second is $\frac{x^2+2}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}.$ The factor $|x|$ is already outside the second blank; it must not be removed or counted twice. This derivative applies for $|x|>1.$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u(x)=\operatorname{arccsc}x$ and $v(x)=e^{2x}+1.$ We have

$$
u'(x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}},\qquad v'(x)=2e^{2x}.
$$

The factor $2$ in $v'(x)$ comes from differentiating the exponent $2x.$ Applying the quotient rule,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}\\
&=\frac{-\frac{e^{2x}+1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}-2e^{2x}\operatorname{arccsc}x}{(e^{2x}+1)^2}\\
&=-\frac{1}{(e^{2x}+1)|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}-\frac{2e^{2x}\operatorname{arccsc}x}{(e^{2x}+1)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both terms carry a minus sign: $u'(x)$ is negative, and the quotient rule subtracts $u(x)v'(x).$ The absolute value must be retained for negative as well as positive $x.$ The derivative applies for $|x|>1.$

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u(x)=\operatorname{arccot}x$ and $v(x)=3x.$ Their derivatives are

$$
u'(x)=-\frac{1}{1+x^2},\qquad v'(x)=3.
$$

Applying the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}\\
&=\frac{\left(-\frac{1}{1+x^2}\right)\,\left(3x\right)-\left(\operatorname{arccot}x\right)\,\left(3\right)}{\left(3x\right)^{2}}\\
&=-\frac{\frac{1}{1+x^2}}{3x}-\frac{\left(\operatorname{arccot}x\right)\,\left(3\right)}{\left(3x\right)^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative applies wherever the original denominator is nonzero.

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u(x)=x^2+5x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{arcsec}x.$ Their derivatives are

$$
u'(x)=2x+5,\qquad v'(x)=\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}.
$$

Applying the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}\\
&=\frac{\left(2x+5\right)\,\left(\operatorname{arcsec}x\right)-\left(x^2+5x\right)\,\left(\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}\right)}{\left(\operatorname{arcsec}x\right)^{2}}\\
&=\frac{2x+5}{\operatorname{arcsec}x}-\frac{\left(x^2+5x\right)\,\left(\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}\right)}{\left(\operatorname{arcsec}x\right)^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative applies where $|x|>1$ and the original denominator is nonzero.

Separate the supplied reciprocal factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\left(2x+5\right)\,\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{arcsec}x}\right)\\
&\quad -\left(\frac{x^2+5x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\right)\,\left(\frac{1}{|x|\left(\operatorname{arcsec}x\right)^{2}}\right)\end{aligned}.
$$

The first blank is $2x+5$ and the second is $\frac{x^2+5x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}.$ The factor $|x|$ is already supplied outside the second blank.

title: Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions Using the Quotient Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we let $u(x) = \operatorname{arcsec}  x$ and $v(x) = \operatorname{arccsc}  x$, and apply the quotient rule.

We use the formulae

$$
u'(x) =  \dfrac 1 {|x| \sqrt {x^2 - 1}}	\quad \text{and} \quad	v'(x) = -\dfrac 1 {|x| \sqrt {x^2 - 1}}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The inverse secant derivative and chain rule give

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{arcsec}(u(x))=
\frac{u'(x)}{|u(x)|\sqrt{u(x)^2-1}}.
$$

Here $u(x)=x^2$ and $u'(x)=2x$. The real domain of the product is $x\geq1$, and we differentiate on $x>1$. Thus $|x^2|=x^2$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{arcsec}(x^2)
&=\frac{2x}{x^2\sqrt{x^4-1}}\\
&=\frac{2}{x\sqrt{x^4-1}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now apply the product rule, using $(\ln x)'=1/x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)&=\frac{1}{x}\operatorname{arcsec}(x^2)
 +\ln(x)\frac{2}{x\sqrt{x^4-1}}\\
&=\frac{\operatorname{arcsec}(x^2)}{x}
 +\frac{2\ln(x)}{x\sqrt{x^4-1}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The chain factor $2x$ differentiates the argument $x^2$; it does not replace that argument inside inverse secant.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsec} ({x}^{3}-6x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{|{x}^{3}-6x|\sqrt{({x}^{3}-6x)^{2}-1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-6x) \\  & =\frac{1}{|{x}^{3}-6x|\sqrt{({x}^{3}-6x)^{2}-1}}\cdot (3{x}^{2}-6) \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}-6}{|{x}^{3}-6x|\sqrt{({x}^{3}-6x)^{2}-1}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line to the curve at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1)\text{ } & =\frac{3(1)^{2}-6}{|{1}^{3}-6(1)|\sqrt{({1}^{3}-6(1))^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{|-5|\sqrt{(1-6)^{2}-1}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{5\sqrt{24}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{5\sqrt{4\cdot 6}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{5\cdot \sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{5\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{10\sqrt{6}} \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{10\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{60} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$
